extracted.intended_audience: writers, literary critics, and educated readers interested in prose style, allegory, and literary evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging and producing effective prose, rhetoric, and allegory — focusing on qualities such as observation, breadth of mind, use of wit and analogy, imagination subordinated to reason, accessibility, and internal coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keen observation and minuteness of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer should notice 'no nice feature of character, no peculiarity in the ordering of a house, a garden, or a court-masque' — a fine tact in observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued as a core quality: close perception of small features that give life to prose. Bacon's Essays are cited as abundant proofs of this quality. Anti-pattern: carelessness about particulars that makes scenes and characters feel generic or flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplitude of comprehension (breadth and integrative knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: A large mind that 'takes in at once all the domains of science' and knows the mutual relations of all departments of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer authors who can connect varied fields and give comparative, global bearings rather than only narrow expertise. Example: Bacon's aim to 'take all knowledge to be my province.' Anti-pattern: narrow specialist detail that fails to relate to wider human concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, concision, and aphoristic compression
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to 'pack thought close, and render it portable' — compressing much thought into small space with memorable aphorisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praised passages (e.g., Bacon's essay extracts) exemplify economical, dense writing that rewards close reading. Anti-pattern: prolixity or diffuse exposition that dilutes key insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eloquence and rhetorical adornment used to illuminate truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of rhetoric to 'illustrate and decorate truth' — wit and eloquence should illuminate, not merely entertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical devices are praised when they make 'obscure truth plain' or 'fix in the mind for ever' ideas that would otherwise be transient. Scoring note: elegance that aids understanding scores highly; mere ornament that obscures substance scores poorly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit and analogy used responsibly (distinguish illustration from argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit and analogy are powerful but must be discriminated: 'analogies which are arguments from analogies which are mere illustrations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good analogies illuminate without being mistaken for proof. Anti-examples: Bacon's occasional overreliance on resemblances (e.g., deriving political theories from pyramids or finance from evaporation) shows how analogies can mislead when treated as arguments rather than illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑contentious, invitational tone (persuasive without polemic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting ideas as suggestions to 'weigh and consider' rather than engaging in controversy — 'conquers with chalk and not with steel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judicious, non‑combative manner can carry a revolution of thought more effectively than aggressive disputation. Anti-pattern: needlessly contentious or polemical writing that closes readers off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination disciplined by reason (vision with plausibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rich imagination that is 'thoroughly subjugated' to good sense — visions that exclude the impossible and remain within plausible bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Celebrate visionary passages (e.g., Bacon's New Atlantis) that are bold yet exclude what 'can be pronounced impossible.' Anti-pattern: fantastic inventions that violate plausibility and thereby undercut credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and prophetic scope anchored in method
rubrics_metrics.description: Bold, original thinking and 'prophetic' views are admirable when grounded in careful induction and discernment of what is feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that open new vistas while showing 'nice discernment' about limits of possibility; scoring favors proposals with both imagination and methodological grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility to ordinary readers (exoteric clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addressing 'plain men' in language everybody understands so that the public can 'judge for themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that make complex ideas intelligible to a broad readership (as Bacon's Essays do) are commended. Anti-pattern: unnecessarily abstruse prose that requires gatekeeping expertise to appreciate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional and human interest in allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegory should produce strong human interest and involve the feelings, not only the understanding; the Pilgrim's Progress 'possesses a strong human interest' and moves readers to tears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer allegories that make readers care about personified experiences; avoid the 'fault of tediousness' where allegory appeals only to intellect and not to feeling (e.g., some of Spenser's allegorical passages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete personification of abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning abstractions into vivid persons and scenes so that 'the imaginations of one mind should become the personal recollections of another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bunyan praised for making personifications into men with dramatic effect; this technique increases empathy and memorability. Anti-pattern: converting images into mere abstractions (e.g., French-school tendency) that make them cold and lifeless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency and coherence in allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain logical and symbolic consistency within the allegorical framework; avoid glaring inconsistencies (e.g., Faithful's martyrdom vs. symbolic river of death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some inconsistencies are perhaps inevitable, but major symbolic contradictions weaken allegory. Comparative note: even celebrated allegories contain lapses, so consistency should be balanced with other virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and balance of visual/illustrative detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations and descriptive detail should support, not overwhelm, the central figures and themes (criticizing engravings that make landscape overpower characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mr. Martin's pictures are faulted for letting landscape and ornament 'draw away all attention from the central figure' — avoid allowing accessories to eclipse the main subject. Scoring: imagery should be proportioned to narrative focus.
